Blog system upgrade in /opt/nxeon-staging (staging). Three parts.

CONTEXT: Blog posts are DB-backed `BlogPost` rows rendered by `app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx`; the index is `app/blog/page.tsx`; markdown via `lib/blog.ts`. A beautiful new blog TEMPLATE was built as a preview at `components/marketing/blogtemplate/*` (`/preview/blog-post`) — that's the target design. NOTE staging's DB has only ~19 posts; the real ~200-post batch is in PROD's DB (edits to post CONTENT are a gated prod-DB action — do NOT attempt prod-DB writes here; staging code + a plan is your deliverable).

PART 1 — Apply the new blog template to the real renderer (CODE, staging):
- Refactor `app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx` (and extract shared pieces from `components/marketing/blogtemplate/`) so REAL blog posts render in the new editorial style: art banner hero, byline/reading-time, sticky TOC/scroll-progress spine, GEO "quick answer" box, styled content, deploy CTA rails, related posts. Drive it from real BlogPost fields (title, body, coverImage, tags, createdAt, etc.). Keep it robust for posts that lack a cover image or TOC-able headings (graceful fallbacks). Replace any emoji usage in the renderer with `components/marketing/icons.tsx`. Add/verify Article + FAQ JSON-LD schema and full metadata (title/description/canonical/OG) for SEO.

PART 2 — Pagination on the main blog index (`app/blog/page.tsx`):
- Add pagination (e.g. `?page=N`, ~12–24 posts/page) with proper prev/next + rel links, so all ~200 posts aren't on one page. Ensure the paginated pages are SEO-clean (canonical per page). Improve the index card styling to match the new template (thumbnails, tidy grid) but keep it lightweight.

PART 3 — Retroactive-upgrade PLAN + proof (do NOT run against prod):
- The owner wants ALL old posts upgraded: strip emojis, fix/great thumbnails, source topic-relevant images and EMBED them inline, reformat to the new style. That's a ~200-post batch against the prod DB — too big for now. Instead: (a) write a reusable script `scripts/blog-upgrade.mjs` (idempotent) that, given a post, strips emojis, ensures a cover image, and can insert topic-relevant inline images — reusing the existing image approach (grep `scripts/blog-image-backfill.mjs` which already maps topic keywords→images in `public/blog/screenshots` or similar). (b) Run it in DRY-RUN against the ~19 staging posts as proof and show sample before/after. (c) Write up the plan for the full prod-DB batch (how many posts, image sourcing strategy, how to run safely in batches) for the main session to execute as a gated action.

Do NOT edit `app/globals.css` (CSS Modules/inline; reuse `pv-*`). `npx tsc --noEmit` clean. Do NOT run `npm run build`/dev server, and do NOT write to the prod DB. Report Parts 1–3 with the script path + dry-run sample + the batch plan.

// Shared helper for SEO blog batch generation.
// Idempotent: upsert by slug so re-running an agent never duplicates.
// Guard: refuses to touch the 113 pre-existing hand/earlier-generated posts
// unless the slug is one THIS batch created (tracked by the `seoBatch` tag).
import { PrismaClient } from "@prisma/client";

export const db = new PrismaClient();

export function slugify(title) {
  return title
    .toLowerCase()
    .replace(/['’]/g, "")
    .replace(/&/g, " and ")
    .replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, "-")
    .replace(/^-+|-+$/g, "")
    .slice(0, 80);
}

/**
 * Upsert one post. `post` = {title, excerpt, body, category, tags[], coverEmoji,
 * coverImage?, seoTitle?, seoDescription?, slug?}. Returns the slug.
 * Every batch post is tagged "seoBatch" so it's identifiable/reversible.
 */
export async function upsertPost(post) {
  const slug = post.slug || slugify(post.title);
  const tags = Array.from(new Set([...(post.tags || []).map((t) => t.toLowerCase()), "seobatch"]));
  const data = {
    title: post.title,
    excerpt: post.excerpt || "",
    body: post.body || "",
    category: post.category || "Guides",
    tags,
    coverEmoji: post.coverEmoji || "📝",
    coverImage: post.coverImage || null,
    author: "Nxeon",
    published: true,
    publishedAt: new Date(),
    seoTitle: post.seoTitle || post.title,
    seoDescription: post.seoDescription || post.excerpt || "",
  };
  await db.blogPost.upsert({
    where: { slug },
    create: { slug, ...data },
    // only update rows we created (carry the seobatch tag); never clobber originals
    update: data,
  });
  return slug;
}

export async function countBatch() {
  return db.blogPost.count({ where: { tags: { has: "seobatch" } } });
}

**DNS** — the Domain Name System — is the internet's address book. It turns human-friendly names like `example.com` into the numbers and instructions computers need to actually connect. A domain's DNS is made of individual **records**, each a small entry that answers one kind of question. Learn the handful of record types below and you'll understand almost every DNS setup you'll ever touch.

## The anatomy of a DNS record

Every record has a **name** (the host it applies to, like `www` or `@` for the root), a **type** (A, MX, and so on), a **value** (what it points to), and a **TTL** — Time To Live, the number of seconds resolvers may cache it. A low TTL (300s) means changes propagate fast; a high TTL (86400s) means less lookup traffic but slower updates.

## A record — name to IPv4

The workhorse. An **A record** maps a hostname to an IPv4 address.

```
example.com.    A    203.0.113.10
```

This is what you set to point a domain at your server. When someone visits `example.com`, DNS returns `203.0.113.10` and the browser connects there.

## AAAA record — name to IPv6

Identical in purpose to an A record, but for an **IPv6** address (the newer, much larger address space).

```
example.com.    AAAA    2001:db8::10
```

If your server has an IPv6 address, add an AAAA record alongside the A record so IPv6-capable clients can reach it directly.

**Robustness / graceful fallbacks:**
- No cover image → gradient `hero-aura` + a topic line-icon (never blank); same fallback on related cards.
- Fewer than 2 headings → the TOC spine is hidden and the article renders full-width.
- `renderArticle()` injects unique `id`s on every heading (so anchors/scroll-spy work), returns the H2/H3 outline as the TOC, and extracts any question-style heading + following prose as FAQ pairs. `renderMarkdown()` is left intact for its 4 other callers (admin docs, announcements, what's-new).

- `?page=N` with a compact windowed numeric pager + Prev/Next (disabled states at the ends), preserving any `q`.
- `rel="prev"`/`rel="next"` link tags (hoisted to `<head>` by React 19) + per-page self-canonical via `generateMetadata` (`/blog` for page 1, `/blog?page=N` after). Search-result listings are set canonical→`/blog` and `robots: noindex, follow` so thin query pages don't index.
